subject: Pharmacology
summary: Potassium iodide is a thyroid blocker used after radioactive iodine exposure. It prevents uptake by the gland and reduces radiation‑induced cancer risk. It is also used in fungal skin infections in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Potassium iodide (KI) is a simple salt that blocks radioactive iodine uptake by the thyroid and is also used topically for cutaneous fungal infections.
Not applicable – KI is a drug, not an organism.
Not applicable – KI is a medication.
KI itself does not cause disease; it is used to prevent radiation‑induced thyroiditis and to treat cutaneous fungal infections.
Identify exposure to radioactive iodine or cutaneous fungal infection.

t.b: Was the patient exposed to 131I? A positive history triggers KI administration.
Does the lesion show fungal elements? A positive culture confirms cutaneous candidiasis.

sections.p: For radiation exposure, give saturated KI 24–48 h after exposure to block uptake. For cutaneous fungal infection, apply saturated KI solution to lesions.

t.b: Check TSH and free T4 to monitor for hypothyroidism after KI.
Confirms fungal etiology; guides duration of topical KI.

sections.p: Remember KI is only protective if started within 24–48 h of exposure. It is not a substitute for iodine‑deficient diets or for treating systemic fungal disease.
b: KI must be started early after exposure
Do not use KI in patients with iodine allergy

t.b: Why must KI be given within 48 h? Early administration blocks most radioactive iodine uptake.

whenToSeekHelp: Radiation exposure with delayed KI administration
Severe skin ulceration or systemic spread of fungal infection

faq.q: Can KI be used for all radioactive iodine exposures?
faq.a: Only if exposure is to 131I and KI is started within 24–48 h.

faq.q: Is KI safe for pregnant women?
faq.a: It is used in pregnancy for radiation protection, but avoid if iodine allergy exists.
Use other iodine‑based solutions or defer until a source is available; monitor thyroid function closely.
